newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up in languid pre-holiday trade.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up in languid pre-holiday trade.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher in extremely light trading on Monday as investors put final touches on their holiday trading strategies and then jumped to the sidelines ahead of the Christmas holiday on Wednesday.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 8/32 at 98-28/32 to yield 6.59 percent. The two-year note rose was flat at 99-26/32, yielding 5.85 percent.
The market spent most of the day in a lull as a few active players struggled to find firm bids to close the deals. The session was mostly dominated by professionals.
"Trading has been pretty lethargic and is quite light," said Cary Leahey, senior economist and senior vice president at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
Analysts said most investors had probably squared their positions and are now waiting for the holidays. Retailers, money managers, hedge funds and foreign players were said to be mostly sidelined.
Many players were actually taking days or even the entire week off ahead of the Christmas holiday. "Our staff is pretty thin this week," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.

The economic indicators issued on Monday were considered mostly market-friendly. The session started with the release of a 0.5-percent rise in personal income in November. Spending was up 0.5 percent and the savings rate was at 5.0 percent.

"These numbers are consistent with a moderate economy and nothing more than that. It's saying to you the income will not support a rapid growth in consumption," said William Griggs, managing director at consulting firm Griggs and Santow Inc.
"The consumer .. is behaving very moderately. He's cautious in spending," Griggs added.
The market also learned that the Univeristy of Michigan's consumer sentiment index fell to 96.9 in the final December reading against 99.2 in the final November report.
Analysts took the numbers as an indication that the Christmas shopping season may be good, but it is unlikely to be terrific.
"This is not going to be a gang-buster Christmas. It's going to be a good Christmas, but not a great one," said the head of a Treasury trading desk at a major foreign investment bank.
Analysts said the data released on Monday were consistent with an overall Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth rate between 2.0 and 3.0 percent in the fourth quarter.
Looking ahead, analysts said the market was expected to remain fairly quiet until the end of the year. "Nothing major is really expected to happen between now and year-end," the head trader said.
On Christmas Eve (Tuesday), the market will have an abbreviated session. Business is expected to shut down at 1400 EST/1900 GMT.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up four basis points at 4.95 percent. The six-month bill rate rose three points to 5.09 percent. The year bill rate was up one point at 5.22 percent.
The five-year note traded up 2/32 at 99-31/32 to yield 6.13 percent. The ten-year note closed up 4/32 at 101-4/32, yielding 6.34 percent.
